name: Colourisation
longDescription:
Turns black-and-white film scans, old broadcasts and home movies into colour. A neural network trained on over a million colour photographs judges what colour each thing in the picture probably was — skin, sky, foliage, clothing — from its shapes and shading alone.

Only the colour is added: the brightness of every pixel stays exactly as it was, so no detail is lost or invented. The colours are the network's best guess, not a record of the original, and it can be wrong about anything whose colour could have been anything, such as clothes or cars. Each frame's colour is steadied against its neighbours so it doesn't flicker, and it runs before Color Correction, so you can grade the result there.

If the video already has colour, that colour is replaced by the network's.

The models are separate downloads, free for any use. DDColor (220 MB) gives vivid, natural colour. DeOldify Video (870 MB) is more muted and was trained to stay steady on video. On a Mac they run on the graphics card and Neural Engine, on Windows on any DirectX 12 graphics card, and otherwise on the CPU, which is much slower.

ui.label: Render Size
ui.description: The size (in pixels, square) the network sees the picture at. 512 is what DDColor was made for; smaller is faster and can give more uniform colour, larger is slower. The colour is scaled to the video's own size either way

ui.label: Render Factor
ui.description: DeOldify's render resolution: the network sees a square 16 times this many pixels across (21 = 336 pixels, its default for video). Higher picks up smaller things and tends to steadier colour, but is slower and can wash colour out

ui.label: Colour Strength
ui.description: How much of the predicted colour is applied. 1 is the network's colour; lower fades it toward black and white, higher makes it more saturated

ui.label: Steady Colour
ui.description: How many frames either side each frame's colour is averaged with, wherever the picture did not move, so colour doesn't flicker from frame to frame. 0 colours every frame on its own; more is steadier on still shots and slower to start a preview
